meta.title: The Name for What You've Been Doing
meta.summary: Voice leading defined as one principle rather than two rules, then traced through chapter 2's C-F-G-C and chapter 3's Am-F-C-G to find where it holds and where it honestly can't.

spans.text: Voice leading is choosing how each note of a chord moves to the next chord so the individual lines move as little as possible. You've been doing it since chapter 2, two chapters before this pathway had a word for it.
One reminder before any of that: a position like
means string 3, fret 5; a chart is six slots, low E first, with

It's one idea, not two rules to juggle. The smallest possible move is no move at all, so look first for a note the next chord already has — a

— and leave that finger exactly where it is. Only then do you move everything else, and each of those notes moves as little as it can. Holding a common tone isn't a separate rule sitting next to "move a short distance"; it's the same rule, since zero beats one.
Chapter 2 played this without naming it.

Here's the honest limit, and it's worth stating plainly.
on strings 3, 2 and 1 — the biggest jump either example makes.

on string 1 — a different pitch on a different string. A common tone can only be held if it's the same pitch on the same string. When it isn't, you slide the whole shape, and that isn't a failure of the rule — it's the rule reporting, honestly, that there was nothing to hold.

Why it matters on a guitar rather than just on paper: less distance is less chance of landing late, and a finger that doesn't move is an anchor the rest of the hand settles around. That's the mechanical argument chapters 2 and 3 made by feel. Now it has a name.
Used as a procedure, it's three steps: name the next chord, find every copy of it on the string set your hand is already on, and take the nearest one. That's what the ladder below draws for

major on strings 1-2-3: first inversion low at fret 1 to 2, second inversion at fret 5 to 6, root position at fret 8 to 10, and first inversion again at fret 13 to 14 — one cycle of the same three notes, climbing the neck, repeating an octave up. It has no play button; the ladder is a map, not something you listen to.
